The cloud launches a server in minutes but **widens the attack surface**: permanent exposure (Internet, APIs, privileged accounts), fast elasticity, shared responsibility. Consequences: controls built in by design, continuous inventory + logs + monitoring, and tight control of permissions, costs, regions and evidence. Cloud security is **not a single product**.

Define cloud computing and list its 5 essential characteristics.

According to NIST, the cloud is a model for on-demand network access to a pool of configurable resources, rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort. Its 5 characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. Each one creates a risk: unapproved resources, Internet or API exposure, isolation and data, unhardened new assets, costs and abuse. So security must be built in by design and automated.
What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS? Give an AWS example.

The more the service is managed, the more responsibilities the provider takes on. In IaaS (e.g. EC2), the customer manages the OS, middleware, applications and data. In PaaS (e.g. Elastic Beanstalk), AWS manages the platform, and the customer keeps their code, data and configurations. In SaaS (e.g. WorkSpaces, according to the course), the application is complete: the customer mostly manages access, their data and settings. In every case, data and identities remain with the customer.
What are the deployment models and how do you choose?

There are four models: public (multi-tenant at a public provider), private (resources dedicated to one organization), community (shared by a community with common needs) and hybrid (a combination of several clouds). The choice depends on the data processed, compliance requirements, cost and the level of control wanted. For example, a bank keeps its customer database private and uses the public cloud for traffic peaks: that is a hybrid model. The integration between the two worlds must then be monitored.
Which security questions should you ask before adopting the cloud?

I ask five questions: which data will be processed (sensitivity, personal data), which services will be exposed (APIs, administrator access), what level of availability is expected (RTO/RPO, multi-AZ, backups), which obligations apply (GDPR, PCI DSS, contracts, location) and who operates what. The decision is secure if it combines business value, accepted risk, available controls, controlled cost and demonstrable compliance.
Why is cloud security so important?

Because the cloud speeds up innovation but widens the attack surface. Services are permanently exposed through the Internet and APIs, resources appear quickly (elasticity) and responsibility is shared. The major risks often come from IAM, misconfigurations, APIs and lack of visibility. Cloud security is not a single product; it is a set of architecture, configuration, monitoring and governance decisions.
Confusing the service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) with the deployment model (public/private/community/hybrid): they are not the same axes.
Believing that with SaaS the customer has nothing left to secure: they remain responsible for their data, users and settings.
Believing that a private cloud is necessarily on-premises: it can be hosted by a third party; what matters is that it is dedicated to one organization.

Thinking cloud security can be bought as a single product: it rests on architecture, configuration, monitoring and governance decisions.
Which risk is associated with elasticity?

When resources are created quickly and automatically, new assets can appear without hardening. Costs and abuse belong to measured service, isolation to resource pooling, and unapproved resources to self-service.

Cloud security objectives: beyond the CIA triad
In the cloud, the CIA triad is no longer enough: you must also prove (traceability), control the bill (cost), grow without creating flaws (scalability) and comply with the law (compliance).
The problem: why 7 objectives and not 3?

The **CIA** triad remains the foundation. But the cloud is shared, elastic, billed by usage and subject to laws: the course adds **4 objectives** (traceability, controlled cost, secure scalability, compliance) for operational and financial security.
The 7 cloud security objectives: click each branch
Continuous access to services. Threats: DDoS, zone or region outage, accidental deletion. Countermeasures: multi-AZ with tested failover, Shield, backups and DRP.
Data and configurations not altered without authorization. Threats: injection, modified network rules, uncontrolled images or IaC. Countermeasures: TLS, hashing, versioning, code review.
Protecting sensitive data. Threats: public bucket, stolen keys or secrets, exfiltration. Countermeasures: encryption, KMS, least-privilege IAM, DLP.
Reliable evidence of access, actions and changes. Threats: missing or deleted logs, late detection. Countermeasures: centralized immutable logs, reliable timestamping, SIEM, alerts.
Preventing abuse that blows up the bill. Threats: cryptojacking, DDoS, mass creation of resources. Countermeasures: budgets, quotas, alerts, anomaly detection.
Scaling up without spreading flaws. Threats: unhardened new nodes, poorly propagated secrets. Countermeasures: tested IaC templates, CI/CD scans, tag-based policies.

Aligning usage with laws, contracts and standards. Threats: data outside the jurisdiction, GDPR or PCI DSS non-compliance, no evidence. Countermeasures: AWS Config, audits, Privacy and Security by Design.
